title: Opportunity Cost and the Margin
bigQuestion: When you choose one thing, how do you measure what that choice really cost you?

story.title: The Shift or the Game
story.kicker: A Peoria junior gets two offers for the same Saturday afternoon and has to work out what each one really costs.
paragraphs: Devon works weekends at a hardware store in Peoria for $15 an hour. On Thursday his manager stopped him by the paint counter. A coworker was sick, and could Devon cover a six-hour shift on Saturday, noon to six? That was $90. Devon said he would let her know by Friday. The problem was the calendar on his phone. Saturday at two o'clock, his sister Kiara's basketball team was playing for the conference championship, and on Monday he had already paid $10 for a student ticket.

At lunch he asked his friends. Luis said the choice was easy, because the ticket was already paid for, so the game was basically free. Aaliyah said that was backward. The game was not free at all; it would cost him the whole $90 he could have earned. Luis said she was counting money Devon never had. They argued until the bell, and Devon walked to class more confused than before.

That night he asked his dad. His dad did not answer the question. He asked a different one. If there were no game, what would you do with Saturday afternoon? Devon said he would take the shift, easily. Then that is what the game costs you, his dad said. Not the ticket. The ticket is gone whether you go or not. The game costs you the shift. And the shift costs you the game, which is the last one Kiara plays before she graduates.

Devon had other numbers in his head too. He had $480 saved toward a $1,200 used car, and $90 would move him closer. But he had already worked 14 hours that week, plus practice, plus a chemistry lab report due Monday. The first hours of work each week felt easy. Another six on top of everything else felt different. Was one more shift worth as much as the first one had been?

By Friday afternoon Devon had an answer, and he texted his manager. He had not found a choice without a cost, because there was none. He had found a way to see the cost clearly. This chapter gives you the same tools: opportunity cost, the production possibilities curve, thinking at the margin, ignoring sunk costs, and the reason people specialize and trade.
story.think: Luis says the game is free, and Aaliyah says it costs $90. Who is right, and what should Devon do about the $10 ticket when he decides?

lessons.title: Every Choice Is a Trade-Off
lessons.mainIdea: Because resources are scarce, choosing one option always means giving up others; that exchange is called a trade-off.
reading: It is Friday night, and you have three free hours. You could babysit for a neighbor and earn $45. You could go to a movie with friends for $15. Or you could stay home and sleep. You cannot do all three in the same three hours. Whatever you pick, you give up the rest. Economists call this a *trade-off*: giving up some of one thing to get more of another. Each option you could choose is an *alternative*.

Businesses face trade-offs too. A restaurant with 2,000 square feet must decide how much space goes to tables and how much to the kitchen. More tables mean more customers at once, but a smaller kitchen that cooks more slowly. An Illinois farmer with 500 acres decides how many to plant in corn and how many in soybeans. Every acre planted in corn is an acre not planted in soybeans. The land is fixed, so more of one crop means less of the other.

Governments make the largest trade-offs. Economists often describe a nation's budget as a choice between *guns and butter*: spending on defense versus spending on goods for daily life. A dollar spent on a fighter jet cannot also pay for a school lunch. Trade-offs also involve time. Suppose a pair of shoes costs $5 less at a store 40 minutes away. Driving there trades 40 minutes of your time for $5. That works out to $5 divided by two-thirds of an hour, or $7.50 an hour.

A common mistake is to think a choice has no trade-off because no money changes hands. Staying home to sleep costs nothing in cash, but it still gives up the $45 and the movie. The first step in any smart decision is to list every realistic alternative before choosing. The next lesson shows how to pick out the one alternative that matters most.

words.d: giving up some of one thing in order to get more of something else
one of the possible options you could choose in a decision
a shorthand for a nation's trade-off between spending on defense and spending on everyday goods

look.title: Three Free Hours
look.text: You have three free hours on Friday night. You could babysit and earn $45, see a movie with friends for $15, or finish a history project due Monday. Your friends will be at the movie again next week, but the babysitting offer is only for this Friday.
look.prompt: List the trade-off in each choice. Which option would you pick, and what are you giving up to get it?

check.q: An Illinois farmer has 500 acres and plants 300 in corn. Why is this a trade-off?
choices: The 300 acres of corn cannot also be planted in soybeans
Corn always sells for more than soybeans
The farmer must pay taxes on the corn
The farmer will buy more land next year
check.why: The land is fixed at 500 acres. Every acre used for corn is an acre given up for soybeans, which is what a trade-off means.

check.q: A store 40 minutes away sells the same shoes for $5 less. If you drive there, about what are you earning per hour of your time?
check.why: 40 minutes is two-thirds of an hour. $5 divided by 2/3 equals $7.50 per hour.

check.q: Which statement about trade-offs is correct?
choices: Only choices that cost money involve trade-offs
Choices that use time or space involve trade-offs even when no money is spent
Governments do not face trade-offs because they can raise taxes
Trade-offs disappear when a person has enough income
check.why: Time, space and land are scarce just like money. Using them for one thing means giving up something else.

lessons.title: The Next-Best Alternative
lessons.mainIdea: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative you give up, not a list of everything you did not choose.
reading: Go back to Friday night. Suppose you rank your options: first, the movie; second, babysitting for $45; third, sleeping. If you choose the movie, what did it cost? The *opportunity cost* of a choice is the value of the *next-best alternative* you give up. Here that is the babysitting. It is not the babysitting plus the sleep, because in those three hours you could only have done one of them. Listing every option you skipped is the most common mistake with this idea.

Opportunity cost counts both what you pay and what you give up. The movie ticket is $15. By going, you also give up $45 of babysitting pay. Measured in dollars, the movie costs you $15 plus $45, or $60. That is why a movie can feel cheap to a student with no job offer and expensive to one who turned down paid work for it. The price is the same for both. The opportunity cost is not.

The classic example is college. Suppose a year at a state university has tuition and fees of $12,000 and books of $1,200 (example figures). A student who goes full time also gives up a job that would have paid $30,000. Those lost wages are called *forgone earnings*. The yearly cost of college is $12,000 plus $1,200 plus $30,000, or $43,200. Food and rent are not added, because the student would pay for them either way.

Opportunity cost is personal because each person's next-best alternative is different. A star athlete offered a professional contract gives up far more to attend college than a student with no such offer. None of this says college, or a movie, is a bad choice. It says the choice is worth it only when its benefits are larger than its full opportunity cost. Seeing that cost clearly is the first habit of economic thinking.

words.d: the value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice
the option you would have chosen if your first choice were not available
income you give up by spending time on something other than paid work

look.title: The Same Movie, Two Prices
look.text: Jada and Marcus both go to the same $15 movie on Friday night. Jada had no other plans and would have watched TV at home. Marcus turned down a three-hour shift at a restaurant that pays $14 an hour to go.
look.prompt: What is the opportunity cost of the movie for each of them, in dollars? Why are the two costs different when the ticket price is the same?

check.q: Keisha ranks her Saturday options: 1. a volunteer event, 2. a paid shift worth $60, 3. a nap. She chooses the volunteer event. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The nap only
The $60 shift and the nap together
Nothing, because volunteering is free
The $60 shift
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best alternative. She could not have done both the shift and the nap in the same time, so the cost is the $60 shift.

check.q: A year of college has $12,000 in tuition and fees, $1,200 in books, and the student gives up a $30,000 job. What is the yearly cost of attending?
check.why: $12,000 plus $1,200 plus $30,000 equals $43,200. Leaving out the forgone earnings gives the wrong $13,200.

check.q: Why are food and rent usually left out of the opportunity cost of college?
choices: They are too small to matter
The government pays for them
The student would pay for them whether or not they attend
They are sunk costs paid before college starts
check.why: Opportunity cost counts only what changes because of the choice. A person must eat and live somewhere either way.

lessons.title: Costs You Pay and Costs You Give Up
lessons.mainIdea: Explicit costs are the money you pay out; implicit costs are the value of what you give up; both count when you judge whether a choice paid off.
reading: Sam spends the summer running a lawn-mowing business in Naperville. He takes in $4,000 from customers. He pays $600 for gas and repairs and $400 to rent a mower. Those payments are *explicit costs*: money actually paid out to someone else. Subtract them from what he took in and Sam's *accounting profit* is $4,000 minus $1,000, or $3,000. On paper, the summer looks like a success.

But Sam had another offer. The city pool wanted him as a lifeguard for the summer at a total of $3,500. By mowing lawns, he gave that up. The value of that lost opportunity is an *implicit cost*: a cost that does not involve paying anyone, but is still real. It is the opportunity cost of using his own time in his own business. Owners often forget it because no bill ever arrives for it.

Economists count both kinds of cost. *Economic profit* is revenue minus explicit costs minus implicit costs. For Sam that is $4,000 minus $1,000 minus $3,500, which equals negative $500. In money terms, Sam would have been $500 better off at the pool. His business earned an accounting profit and an economic loss at the same time. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

Does that mean Sam chose badly? Not necessarily. Maybe he liked being his own boss, or learned skills a lifeguard job would not teach. Those benefits are real even without a price tag. What economic profit does is put the full cost on the table, so Sam can ask whether those other benefits were worth at least $500 to him. That is a much better question than the one the accounting profit answers.

words.d: a cost that involves paying money to someone else, such as rent, wages or supplies
the value of an opportunity given up that involves no payment, such as the wages an owner could earn elsewhere
total revenue minus explicit costs
total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs

look.title: Sam's Summer Business (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one student's summer lawn-mowing business
look.prompt: Which rows are explicit costs and which is an implicit cost? Find the accounting profit and the economic profit. What would the lifeguard pay have to be for economic profit to be zero?

check.q: Using Sam's numbers, what is his accounting profit?
check.why: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs: $4,000 minus $600 minus $400 equals $3,000.

check.q: Which of these is an implicit cost for a person running her own bakery?
choices: The salary she could have earned managing someone else's bakery
The rent she pays for the shop
The flour she buys each week
The wages she pays her helper
check.why: An implicit cost involves no payment. The salary she gives up is the opportunity cost of her own time. The other three are explicit payments.

check.q: A business takes in $50,000, has explicit costs of $30,000, and the owner gave up a $25,000 job. What is its economic profit?
check.why: Economic profit is $50,000 minus $30,000 minus $25,000, which equals negative $5,000, an economic loss.

lessons.title: A Table of Possibilities
lessons.mainIdea: A production possibilities curve shows every combination of two goods an economy can make with all its resources fully used; points on it are efficient.
reading: Imagine a small country that makes only two goods, food and machines. It has a fixed amount of land, workers, tools and know-how. If it puts everything into food, it makes 100,000 tons of food and no machines. If it puts everything into machines, it makes 50,000 machines and no food. Between those extremes lie many mixes. Economists list them in a table and, when they draw them, call the line the *production possibilities curve*, or PPC.

Here is the table for this example, with food in thousands of tons and machines in thousands. Point A: 0 machines, 100 food. Point B: 10 machines, 95 food. Point C: 20 machines, 85 food. Point D: 30 machines, 65 food. Point E: 40 machines, 35 food. Point F: 50 machines, 0 food. Every point in the table uses all of the country's resources. Picture the points on a graph with machines across the bottom and food up the side, joined by a curve that bends outward.

A point on the curve is *efficient*: the country cannot make more of one good without making less of the other. A point inside the curve means resources are being wasted. Suppose the country makes 20 machines and 60 food. Point C shows it could make 20 machines and 85 food, so 25,000 tons of food are being lost. This happens when workers are unemployed or factories sit idle, as in a recession. These are *unemployed resources*.

A point outside the curve is *unattainable* with today's resources and technology. The country cannot make 30 machines and 80 food, because at 30 machines the most food it can make is 65. The PPC turns scarcity into a picture. It shows the limit, the trade-off along that limit, and the waste inside it. It also sets up the next question: why does moving along the curve cost more and more?

words.d: a graph or table showing the combinations of two goods an economy can produce using all its resources
producing the most possible from the resources available, with none wasted
workers, land or machines that are available but not being used to produce anything
describing a combination of goods the economy cannot produce with its current resources and technology

look.title: Food and Machines (example)
look.cite: Made-up production possibilities for a small economy; machines in thousands
look.prompt: Is 40 machines and 30 food efficient, inefficient or unattainable? What about 10 machines and 100 food? Explain each answer using the table.

check.q: Using the table, the country makes 30 machines and 50 food. Which describes this point?
choices: Efficient, because it is on the curve
Unattainable, because it is outside the curve
Inefficient, because 15 more food could be made with 30 machines
Efficient, because it makes some of each good
check.why: At 30 machines the table shows a maximum of 65 food. Making only 50 means 15,000 tons are lost, so the point is inside the curve.

check.q: Which event would most likely move an economy from a point on its PPC to a point inside it?
choices: A recession that leaves many workers unemployed
A new invention that makes farming faster
A decision to make more machines and less food
An increase in the number of workers
check.why: Idle workers are unused resources, so output falls below what the economy could make. The other events either move along the curve or shift it.

check.q: Why is 30 machines and 80 food unattainable in the example?
choices: Because the country prefers food
Because the most food possible with 30 machines is 65
Because 30 machines is more than the country needs
Because all points above 50 food are unattainable
check.why: Point D shows that making 30 machines leaves resources for at most 65 food. Anything beyond that lies outside the curve.

lessons.title: Why the Curve Bows Outward
lessons.mainIdea: Because resources are not equally good at making everything, each extra unit of a good costs more of the other good; this bends the curve outward.
reading: Use the food and machines table to measure the cost of each step. Going from A to B, the country gains 10 machines and gives up 5 food, so each machine costs half a ton of food. From B to C, 10 more machines cost 10 food, or 1 ton each. From C to D, 10 machines cost 20 food, or 2 each. From D to E, they cost 30 food, or 3 each. From E to F, the last 10 machines cost 35 food, or 3.5 each. The more machines the country makes, the more each additional one costs.

This pattern is called the *law of increasing opportunity cost*. The reason is that resources are *specialized*: they are better at some jobs than others. When the country starts making machines, it moves the workers and land best suited to machines and least useful on farms. Little food is lost. But as it keeps going, it must pull in skilled farmers and the richest farmland. Each of those makes few machines and was producing a lot of food.

The increasing cost is what bends the curve outward, away from the origin. If resources were equally good at both jobs, the cost would stay the same at every step and the curve would be a straight line. That is called *constant opportunity cost*. A student splitting study time between two similar subjects might face it: each hour moved from one to the other costs about the same amount of learning in the other.

A common mistake is to read the curve's shape as a statement about what people want. It is not. The PPC shows only what the economy can make. Which point it picks depends on the choices of its people or government. The bow shape tells you something useful for any decision: going all-in on one thing gets expensive, because the last resources you move over are the ones worst suited to it.

words.d: the rule that as production of one good rises, the cost of each extra unit in terms of the other good also rises
workers, land and tools that are much better suited to some kinds of production than to others
a situation in which each extra unit of a good costs the same amount of the other good, giving a straight-line PPC

look.title: Moving the Farmers
look.text: A country decides to double its machine output. The first workers who move from farms to factories are mechanics who worked on tractors. Later the factories need more hands, and the government moves experienced corn growers from the best land in the country into the machine plants.
look.prompt: Which group of workers costs the country more food per machine when they move, and why? Use the idea of specialized resources in your answer.

check.q: In the table, moving from D (30 machines, 65 food) to E (40 machines, 35 food) costs how much food per machine?
choices: 2 tons
0.5 tons
3.5 tons
3 tons
check.why: The country gives up 65 minus 35, or 30 thousand tons of food, for 10 thousand machines. 30 divided by 10 equals 3 tons per machine.

check.q: What causes the law of increasing opportunity cost?
choices: Resources are not equally suited to producing every good
Consumers want more of both goods
Prices rise every year because of inflation
Governments tax the second good more heavily
check.why: The first resources moved are the best fit for the new good. Later ones are worse at it and were more productive where they were, so each unit costs more.

check.q: A PPC is drawn as a straight line. What does that tell you?
choices: The economy is inefficient
The economy is growing
The opportunity cost of each unit stays the same
The economy makes only one good
check.why: A straight line means every step gives up the same amount of the other good, which is constant opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Shifting the Curve Outward
lessons.mainIdea: Economic growth moves the whole curve outward; it comes from more or better resources and technology, and today's choices between capital and consumer goods shape it.
reading: Suppose the country in our example discovers a better way to build machines. With the same workers and land, it can now make 60,000 machines instead of 50,000 if it makes no food, and more machines at every level of food. The whole curve moves outward. Combinations that were unattainable last year are now possible. That outward shift is *economic growth*: an increase in the economy's capacity to produce.

Growth has a few main sources. More resources shift the curve out: more workers, more usable land, more factories. Better technology shifts it out, as when hybrid seed raised corn yields or computers sped up design. More human capital shifts it out, because trained workers produce more in the same hours. A shift can also go inward. A war, a flood or a pandemic that destroys factories or keeps people from working shrinks what the economy can make.

Moving from a point inside the curve to a point on it is not growth. It is putting idle resources back to work. Growth means the limit itself moves. Here is where today's choices matter. *Capital goods* are machines, tools and buildings used to make other things. *Consumer goods* are things people use up directly, like food, clothes and phones. A country that makes more capital goods today gives up some consumption now, but it will have more tools to work with later.

Compare two countries with the same curve this year. Country X chooses 40 percent capital goods and 60 percent consumer goods. Country Y chooses 10 percent capital goods and 90 percent consumer goods. People in Y live better this year. But X is building more factories and equipment, so ten years from now its curve is likely to have moved out much farther. The choice between them is a trade-off between the present and the future, the same one a student makes by studying tonight.

words.d: an increase in an economy's ability to produce goods and services, shown by an outward shift of the PPC
goods such as machines, tools and buildings that are used to produce other goods and services
goods that people buy to use themselves, such as food, clothing and phones

look.title: Two Countries, One Starting Line
look.text: Two countries have identical production possibilities this year. One puts most of its effort into roads, factories, schools and equipment and lives with fewer new consumer goods. The other puts most of its effort into goods people enjoy now, such as clothes, food and entertainment.
look.prompt: Which country's curve is likely to shift out more over ten years, and why? What is the opportunity cost of that growth for the people living there today?

check.q: Which of these would shift a country's PPC outward?
choices: Workers who were unemployed go back to their jobs
A flood destroys several factories
The country decides to make more food and fewer machines
A new technology lets each worker produce more
check.why: Better technology raises the most the economy can make, which moves the curve. Rehiring idle workers moves a point toward the curve but does not move the curve itself.

check.q: A country moves from a point inside its PPC to a point on it. What happened?
choices: It used resources that had been idle
It grew, because its curve shifted outward
Its opportunity costs fell to zero
It discovered new natural resources
check.why: Moving from inside to on the curve means idle resources went back to work. Growth would require the curve itself to move.

check.q: Why might a country that makes more capital goods today have more consumer goods in the future?
choices: Capital goods are cheaper than consumer goods
Capital goods raise future productive capacity, shifting the curve out
Consumer goods cannot be made in the future
Capital goods are not affected by scarcity
check.why: Machines, factories and tools increase what the economy can produce later. The cost is giving up some consumer goods now.

lessons.title: One More Hour, One More Unit
lessons.mainIdea: Most decisions are about a little more or a little less; keep going as long as the marginal benefit of the next step is at least its marginal cost.
reading: A coffee shop closes at 8 p.m. The owner wonders whether to stay open later. The question is not whether the shop should exist, or whether it is profitable overall. The question is about one more hour. In economics, *marginal* means additional or extra. The *marginal benefit* is what you gain from one more unit of something. The *marginal cost* is what you give up for that one more unit. Comparing the two is called thinking at the margin.

Here are the owner's numbers (example figures). Staying open from 8 to 9 would bring in $120 in extra sales. Staying open from 9 to 10 would add $70. From 10 to 11, only $40. Each extra hour costs $60 for a worker, electricity and supplies. The first extra hour adds $120 and costs $60, so it is worth it. The second adds $70 and costs $60, still worth it by $10. The third adds $40 and costs $60, a $20 loss. The owner should close at 10.

The rule is simple. Keep doing more of something as long as the marginal benefit of the next unit is greater than or equal to its marginal cost, and stop when it falls below. Notice that the owner did not look at the average sales for the whole day. A shop that averages $150 an hour over the day can still lose money in its last hour. Mixing up the average with the marginal is a common and costly mistake.

Thinking at the margin also explains a puzzle that Adam Smith noticed. Water is necessary for life and cheap. Diamonds are not necessary and cost a fortune. The answer is that prices reflect the value of one more unit. Water is so plentiful that one more gallon adds little. Diamonds are so scarce that one more is worth a lot. In the story, Devon's next shift was worth less to him than his first because he had already worked 14 hours that week.

words.d: additional or extra; the next unit of something
the extra benefit gained from one more unit of an activity or good
the extra cost of producing or doing one more unit of something

look.title: Staying Open Late (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one coffee shop deciding when to close
look.prompt: Compare each hour's extra sales with its cost. What time should the shop close? If the cost of each extra hour rose to $80, when should it close?

check.q: Extra sales are $120, $70 and $40 for three extra hours, and each hour costs $60. How many extra hours should the shop stay open?
check.why: The first two hours bring in more than their $60 cost. The third brings in $40, less than $60, so the shop should stop after two extra hours.

check.q: Why can a shop that averages $150 in sales per hour still lose money in its last hour?
choices: Average sales are always lower than marginal sales
The average counts only the last hour
The last hour's sales can be far lower than the average
Marginal cost is always zero at night
check.why: The decision about one more hour depends on that hour's sales and cost, not the day's average. Busy hours can hide a slow final hour.

check.q: Why do diamonds cost more than water even though water is more necessary?
choices: Water is produced by the government
Diamonds have a higher total usefulness than water
Water has no opportunity cost
One more diamond is worth much more than one more gallon of plentiful water
check.why: Prices reflect marginal value. Water is plentiful, so an extra gallon adds little. Diamonds are scarce, so an extra one adds a lot.

lessons.title: Sunk Costs Stay Sunk
lessons.mainIdea: A sunk cost has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so it should not affect a decision about what to do next.
reading: You paid $60 for a concert ticket that cannot be refunded or resold. On the night of the show you have a bad cold, it is pouring rain, and a friend invites you to a quiet movie night at her house. Many people drag themselves to the concert anyway, saying they cannot waste $60. But the $60 is gone whether you go or not. It is a *sunk cost*: money, time or effort already spent that cannot be gotten back.

The only question that matters is about the future. Which will you enjoy more tonight, the concert with a cold in the rain or the movie night? Compare only the costs and benefits that still depend on your choice. Economists call those *relevant costs*. The ticket price is not one of them, because nothing you do tonight changes it. In the story, Devon's $10 basketball ticket was sunk too. His real choice was between the game and the $90 shift.

Businesses make the same mistake on a larger scale. Suppose a company has spent $2 million building a new app. Finishing it will take another $1 million, and the company now expects it to earn only $800,000 in sales. Managers who think about the $2 million already spent may push ahead to avoid wasting it. But the $2 million is sunk. Going forward, spending $1 million to earn $800,000 loses $200,000. The right move is to stop.

Letting a sunk cost drive a choice is called the *sunk cost fallacy*. It keeps people in bad investments, failing projects and even classes or teams they no longer want. Ignoring sunk costs is not the same as ignoring lessons. The money spent can teach you something for next time. It just cannot be recovered by spending more. Good decisions look forward, not back.

words.d: a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next
a cost that will change depending on which choice you make, and so should affect the decision
the mistake of continuing something because of what you already spent on it rather than what lies ahead

look.title: Halfway Through the Season
look.text: Rosa paid a $150 nonrefundable fee to join a club volleyball team. Six weeks in, she dreads every practice, and a local restaurant has offered her a job on practice nights paying $12 an hour for 6 hours a week. The season has eight weeks left.
look.prompt: Should the $150 fee affect her choice? List the relevant costs and benefits of staying on the team for the last eight weeks.

check.q: A company has spent $2 million on a project. Finishing costs $1 million more and will bring in $800,000. What should it do?
choices: Finish, so the $2 million is not wasted
Stop, because the extra $1 million will earn back only $800,000
Finish, because $800,000 is a lot of money
Spend more to make the project bigger
check.why: The $2 million is sunk. Looking forward, spending $1 million to earn $800,000 loses $200,000, so stopping is the better choice.

check.q: Which of these is a sunk cost?
choices: A nonrefundable deposit already paid for a trip
The cost of gas for a trip you have not taken yet
Wages you would earn if you skip the trip
The price of a hotel you have not booked
check.why: The deposit is already paid and cannot come back. The others still depend on what you choose, so they are relevant costs.

check.q: Devon paid $10 for a game ticket and was offered a $90 shift at the same time. What should he compare when deciding?
choices: The $10 ticket and the $90 shift
Only the $10 ticket
The value of the game to him and the $90 shift
The $90 shift minus the $10 ticket
check.why: The $10 is sunk whether he goes or not. The live choice is between the value of watching the game and the $90 of pay.

lessons.title: Weighing a Real Decision
lessons.mainIdea: Cost-benefit analysis lists every cost, including opportunity costs, and every benefit of a choice, puts dollar values on what it can, and compares them.
reading: Jordan is a junior deciding whether to take a college course at a community college this summer. The class meets weekday mornings for six weeks. He could work those same hours at a grocery store. To decide, he uses *cost-benefit analysis*: a step-by-step way to weigh a choice. Step one, name the options. Step two, list every cost, including opportunity costs. Step three, list every benefit. Step four, put dollar values on what you can and compare.

The costs, with example figures: tuition of $450 and books of $100, which are explicit. He also gives up 10 hours of work a week for 6 weeks, or 60 hours, at $15 an hour. That is $900 of forgone earnings, an implicit cost. Total cost: $450 plus $100 plus $900, or $1,450. The main benefit: the three credits will transfer to the state university he plans to attend, where the same course would cost about $1,500 in tuition.

Compare. Benefits of about $1,500 minus costs of $1,450 give a *net benefit* of $50. In money terms the class barely wins. That is where the benefits without a price tag come in. Jordan gets a taste of college work, a line on his applications and a lighter load as a freshman. Against that, he loses summer free time and six weeks of work experience. These are *nonmonetary* costs and benefits: real, but hard to put in dollars.

Cost-benefit analysis does not make the decision for you. When the numbers are close, as here, your own values decide. When they are far apart, the numbers usually settle it. Its real power is making you count what people forget: forgone wages, time and the next-best alternative. Governments use the same method, on a bigger scale, when they decide whether a new highway or a flood wall is worth what it costs.

words.d: a method of making a decision by listing and comparing all the costs and benefits of each option
total benefits minus total costs
describing a cost or benefit that is real but not easily measured in money, such as time, stress or experience

look.title: Jordan's Summer Class (example)
look.cite: Made-up figures for one student's summer course decision
look.prompt: Which rows are costs and which is a benefit? Find the net benefit. If Jordan's job paid $20 an hour instead, would the class still come out ahead in money terms?

check.q: Jordan gives up 60 hours of work at $15 an hour. What is his forgone income?
check.why: 60 hours times $15 per hour equals $900. That is an implicit cost of taking the class.

check.q: Total costs are $1,450 and total money benefits are $1,500. What is the net benefit?
check.why: Net benefit is benefits minus costs: $1,500 minus $1,450 equals $50.

check.q: Which item would Jordan list as a nonmonetary benefit of the class?
choices: The $450 tuition
The $900 in wages
Getting used to college-level work
The $1,500 saved at the university
check.why: Experience with college work is a real benefit, but it has no price tag. The other items are measured in dollars.

lessons.title: Why People Specialize
lessons.mainIdea: People and places gain by specializing in what they do at the lowest opportunity cost, even when someone else is better at everything.
reading: Ana and Ben share an apartment and have two hours on Sunday to make sandwiches for the week and fold laundry. In one hour Ana can make 6 sandwiches or fold 12 shirts. Ben can make 2 sandwiches or fold 8 shirts. Ana is faster at both jobs. When a person can produce more of something with the same time, she has an *absolute advantage* in it. Ana has an absolute advantage in both. Does that mean she should do everything?

Look at opportunity cost. For Ana, one sandwich costs 2 shirts, because 12 shirts divided by 6 sandwiches is 2. For Ben, one sandwich costs 4 shirts, because 8 divided by 2 is 4. Ana gives up less to make a sandwich, so she has the *comparative advantage* in sandwiches: the lower opportunity cost. For shirts it flips. One shirt costs Ana half a sandwich, but costs Ben only a quarter of one. Ben has the comparative advantage in folding shirts.

Now compare two plans. If each spends one hour on each job, Ana makes 6 sandwiches and 12 shirts, and Ben makes 2 sandwiches and 8 shirts. Together: 8 sandwiches and 20 shirts. If they *specialize*, Ben folds for both hours, making 16 shirts. Ana makes sandwiches for 90 minutes, which is 9, and folds for 30 minutes, which is 6 shirts. Together: 9 sandwiches and 22 shirts. Same people, same two hours, more of both. That extra output is the gain from *specialization*.

Adam Smith saw the same thing in a pin workshop. He described ten workers who split pin-making into separate steps and together made more than 48,000 pins a day, while one person doing every step alone could hardly make twenty. Splitting a job into steps done by different people is the *division of labor*. It is why a Chicago hospital has surgeons, nurses and billing clerks rather than doctors who do everything. Unit 8 returns to comparative advantage between whole countries.

words.d: the ability to produce more of a good than someone else using the same amount of time or resources
the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else
focusing on producing a narrow range of goods or tasks instead of doing everything yourself
splitting the work of making something into separate steps done by different workers

look.title: Smith on the Division of Labor
look.text: The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour, and the greater part of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which it is any where directed, or applied, seem to have been the effects of the division of labour.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 1, 1776
look.prompt: Smith says dividing work raises both output and skill. How does doing one step over and over make a worker more skilled? Give an example from a job you know.

check.q: In one hour Ana makes 6 sandwiches or folds 12 shirts. What is her opportunity cost of one sandwich?
choices: 6 shirts
0.5 shirts
12 shirts
2 shirts
check.why: In the time it takes to make 6 sandwiches she could fold 12 shirts. 12 divided by 6 equals 2 shirts per sandwich.

check.q: Ana is faster than Ben at both jobs. Why should Ben still fold the shirts?
choices: Ben has the lower opportunity cost for folding shirts
Ben has an absolute advantage in folding
Ana should do both jobs because she is faster
Folding shirts has no opportunity cost
check.why: A shirt costs Ben a quarter of a sandwich and Ana half of one. Ben gives up less, so he has the comparative advantage in folding.

check.q: Without specializing, Ana and Ben make 8 sandwiches and 20 shirts. With specializing, they make 9 and 22. What is the gain?
choices: 2 sandwiches and 1 shirt
1 sandwich and 2 shirts
17 sandwiches and 42 shirts
No gain, because they worked the same hours
check.why: 9 minus 8 is 1 extra sandwich, and 22 minus 20 is 2 extra shirts, from the same two hours of work each.

lessons.title: Trade Makes Both Sides Better Off
lessons.mainIdea: In a voluntary trade both sides expect to gain, because each values what it gets more than what it gives up; trade creates value rather than just moving it.
reading: You buy an iced coffee for $4. You would have paid up to $6 for it on a hot afternoon, so you walk away feeling $2 better off. The shop's cost to make it, counting milk, ice, cup and the worker's time, is $3, so it is $1 better off. Nobody was tricked. Each side gave up something it valued less for something it valued more. That is why a *voluntary exchange* happens at all. Together, the two sides are $3 better off than before.

This means trade is not a *zero-sum* game, where one side's gain is exactly the other's loss. A poker pot is zero-sum: whatever one player wins, the others lose. A voluntary trade is positive-sum. Value is created because the coffee moved from someone who valued it at $3 to someone who valued it at $6. The extra satisfaction both sides get is called the *gains from trade*.

Specialization only works because of trade. Ana makes sandwiches and Ben folds shirts, and then they share. Illinois farmers grow corn and soybeans far beyond what they could eat, then sell the crop and buy trucks, phones and medicine. Chicago became a trading center for exactly this reason. The Chicago Board of Trade, founded in 1848, gave farmers and grain buyers one place to meet and agree on prices. Specializing and trading make people dependent on each other, a condition called *interdependence*.

Trade does not help everyone equally, and later chapters look at who wins and who loses when it grows. A trade can also go wrong when one side is lied to or forced, which is why laws against fraud matter. But the core idea holds. When two people agree freely to a trade, both expect to be better off, or they would say no. That simple fact, repeated millions of times a day, is the engine of a market economy.

words.d: a trade that both sides agree to because each expects to be better off
describing a situation in which one side's gain is exactly equal to the other side's loss
the extra value both sides receive when they trade instead of producing everything themselves
the condition of people and places relying on each other for goods and services

look.title: The Used Bike
look.text: Mia has a used bike she no longer rides. She would sell it for anything above $80. Theo needs a bike to get to his summer job and would pay up to $150. They agree on a price of $110.
look.prompt: How much better off is Mia? How much better off is Theo? What is the total value created by the trade, and why did it happen without anyone forcing it?

check.q: A buyer values a coffee at $6 and pays $4. The shop's cost is $3. What is the total gain from the trade?
check.why: The buyer gains $6 minus $4, or $2. The shop gains $4 minus $3, or $1. Together they gain $3.

check.q: Why is a voluntary trade not a zero-sum game?
choices: Both sides expect to end up better off, so value is created
The seller always gains and the buyer always loses
The government makes sure the gains are equal
Prices never change after the trade
check.why: Each side gives up something it values less for something it values more, so both can gain at once.

check.q: Illinois farmers grow far more corn than they can use and sell it to buy other goods. This shows
choices: a command economy
a zero-sum game
specialization combined with trade
the sunk cost fallacy
check.why: The farmers specialize in what they do well, then trade the surplus for goods others make. That is specialization and trade together.

lessons.title: Investing in Your Own Skills
lessons.mainIdea: Education and training cost tuition plus the pay you give up, and they can raise what you earn for years; weigh the full cost against the expected gain.
reading: Maya is 18 and earns $25,000 a year at a warehouse (all numbers in this lesson are examples). She is thinking about a one-year welding certificate at a community college. Tuition and gear cost $7,000. She would work less during the program and lose about $15,000 in pay. So the full cost is $7,000 + $15,000 = $22,000. The pay she gives up is an opportunity cost, and it is often bigger than the tuition.

Now the benefit. Suppose certified welders near Maya start at $37,000 a year. That is $12,000 more than her warehouse job. Divide the cost by the yearly gain: $22,000 / $12,000 is about 1.8. After about two years of work, the certificate has paid for itself. Every year after that is extra income. Economists call the skills and knowledge a person builds *human capital*, because like a machine it costs money now and pays off later.

There are many paths. A four-year degree costs more and takes longer, but on average it leads to higher pay over a career. An *apprenticeship* lets a person earn a wage while learning a trade, such as electrician or plumber, so the opportunity cost is small. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show every year that workers with more education earn more on average and are unemployed less often. Averages do not decide for any one person, though.

A good decision weighs more than the average. How long will the program take? Will you borrow, and at what interest rate? Do jobs in that field exist where you want to live? Will you finish? A common mistake is to count only tuition and forget the lost pay. Another is to assume a credential guarantees a raise. The *return on investment* is the gain compared with the full cost, and it differs from person to person.

words.d: the skills, knowledge and training a person has that let them produce more and earn more
a training program in which a person earns a wage while learning a trade on the job
the gain from an investment compared with its full cost

look.title: Three Paths After High School (example)
look.cite: Invented figures for practice, not real wages
look.prompt: How much more does welding pay each year than the current job? About how many years does it take to earn back its full cost?

check.q: A one-year program costs $6,000 in tuition. During it, you give up a job that pays $24,000 a year. What is the full cost of the program?
check.why: Full cost = tuition + the pay you give up: $6,000 + $24,000 = $30,000.

check.q: A training program's full cost is $40,000. It raises yearly pay by $10,000. About how many years of work does it take to earn the cost back?
choices: 10 years
40 years
4 years
2 years
check.why: $40,000 / $10,000 per year = 4 years; after that, the extra pay is a gain.

check.q: Which choice is an investment in human capital?
choices: Buying a newer car
Taking a longer vacation
Upgrading a phone plan
Earning an electrician's license through an apprenticeship
check.why: Human capital is skill and knowledge; an apprenticeship builds a trade skill that raises future earnings.

review.q: Priya can go to a party, work a $50 shift, or study, and she ranks them in that order. She goes to the party. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The $50 shift
The shift and studying
Studying only
Nothing, since she enjoyed the party
review.why: Opportunity cost is the single next-best alternative. Her second choice was the $50 shift.

review.q: A business takes in $80,000. It pays $50,000 in rent, wages and supplies, and the owner gave up a $40,000 job. Which is correct?
choices: Accounting profit $30,000 and economic profit $30,000
Accounting profit $30,000 and economic profit -$10,000
Accounting profit -$10,000 and economic profit $30,000
Accounting profit $80,000 and economic profit $40,000
review.why: Accounting profit is $80,000 minus $50,000, or $30,000. Subtracting the $40,000 implicit cost as well gives an economic loss of $10,000.

review.q: On a PPC, moving from 20 to 30 machines lowers food from 85 to 65 units. What is the opportunity cost of each of those 10 machines?
choices: 20 units of food
10 units of food
2 units of food
0.5 units of food
review.why: 20 units of food are given up for 10 machines. 20 divided by 10 equals 2 units of food per machine.

review.q: Which of these would shift a country's production possibilities curve inward?
choices: A rise in the number of trained workers
A move from one point on the curve to another
A decision to produce more capital goods
An earthquake that destroys many factories
review.why: Destroying factories reduces the resources available, so the most the economy can make falls. The other choices keep or expand capacity.

review.q: A tutor charges $20 an hour. For you, a first hour of tutoring before a test is worth $50, a second $25 and a third $15. How many hours should you buy?
review.why: Buy hours while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. The first two hours are worth more than $20; the third is worth only $15.

review.q: You paid $200 for a nonrefundable course. Halfway through, you realize it is not useful and a paid internship is available on the same days. What should you do about the $200?
choices: Finish the course so the $200 is not wasted
Ignore it and compare the rest of the course with the internship
Add it to the value of the internship
Ask for twice as much pay at the internship
review.why: The $200 is a sunk cost. Only the costs and benefits still ahead should decide the choice.

review.q: In an hour, Lena can paint 4 signs or bake 8 pies. Omar can paint 3 signs or bake 3 pies. Who has the comparative advantage in painting signs?
choices: Lena, because she paints more signs per hour
Neither, because they paint at similar speeds
Both of them equally
Omar, because a sign costs him 1 pie while it costs Lena 2 pies
review.why: For Lena a sign costs 8 divided by 4, or 2 pies. For Omar it costs 3 divided by 3, or 1 pie. Omar gives up less, so he has the comparative advantage.

review.q: Mia would sell her bike for anything above $80, and Theo would pay up to $150. They agree on $110. What are the total gains from trade?
review.why: Mia gains $110 minus $80, or $30. Theo gains $150 minus $110, or $40. Together that is $70, the gap between $150 and $80.
